subject: How to perform MGCFA using Lavaan when we have groups of variables and not two different categories.

messages.author: 2afd210174337bb1
messages.subject: How to perform MGCFA using Lavaan when we have groups of variables and not two different categories.
parts:
Hello all,

I want to perform multi group confirmatory factor analysis using
Lavaan. In my case I do not have different groups (i.e., male and
female). I have group of variables. The variables are value
orientations and I want to find out whether the item hypothesized to
load strongly on a value orientation is loading strongly on that
value orientation or not.
My problem is that I can find examples of how to define Lavaan syntax
when we have two different groups such as two schools and male and
female. However I cannot find examples (or have failed to find
examples) of how to write Lavaan syntax that are appropriate for my
situation.
So my question is that how to tell Lavaan that I have a group of
variables and I want to know that how strongly or weakly my items are
loading on each variable (group).

I will appreciate any helpful suggestions.

Best regards,
Faiz.

messages.author: 5b9c62b1c7cbc1e6
messages.subject: Re: How to perform MGCFA using Lavaan when we have groups of variables and not two different categories.
parts:
Faiz,

Unless I'm missing something, it sounds like you want to estimate a CFA with multiple factors--one for each value orientation. The hypothesized model would be that each orientation's items load on that orientation.

Pat

messages.author: 2afd210174337bb1
messages.subject: Re: How to perform MGCFA using Lavaan when we have groups of variables and not two different categories.
parts:
Pat, Thank you for your reply.

 

I am testing Value-Belief-Norm theory. I have performed CFA to test that are hypothesized items loading on the factor (value orientation) they are hypothesized to load. What I am trying to do is to follow the analytical strategy of an influential researcher in my field Linda Steg. In several papers Steg and her colleagues have used Multi Group Method (MGM) CFA to test how each value is loading on various value orientations. Let me Use the value social power as an example to clarify my point.

Social power is an egoistic value and should in theory load strongly on egoistic value orientation. In their papers Steg and colleagues provide corrected correlations of each item with all of the value orientations after performing MGM CFA. For example in the paper I have currently opened in front of me Social power has a correlation of .27 with hedonic value orientation, .01 with altruistic value orientation and .52 with egoistic value orientation (the orientation on which this value should strongly load in theory).

What I am struggling with is that I do not know (or have failed to find out so far) is how to instruct Lavaan to provide loadings of every item on all factors (which in my case are value orientations). Or in other words I can perform a  simple CFA using Lavaan where I get  a loading of an item on a hypothesized factor and I can use criteria  available in the literature to decide whether  the loading suggest that the item  can be used to measure this factor or not. But I do not know how to perform MGM CFA using Lavaan.

The examples of performing multi group CFA using Lavaan I have found on the web have described situations where two categories are present (e.g., male and female).

I hope that I have been able to clearly explain my situation and I hope that I will find a solution.

Sorry for such a long email.

 

Best regards,

Reference:

Hiratsuka, J., Perlaviciute, G., & Steg, L. (2018). Testing VBN theory in Japan: Relationships between values, beliefs, norms, and acceptability and expected effects of a car pricing policy. Transportation research part F: traffic psychology and behaviour, 53, 74-83.

parts:
MGM is in fact kind of a confirmatory centroid component analysis. It is not a SEM method. It is also very simple computationally - you do not need Lavaan for it, even Excel will do the job. For details see e.g. Nunnally & Bernstein (1994), pp. 555-561.
Best regards, Gregor
